rows.selection_reason: 1) Evidence/uncertainty: No experiments have been run, so there is zero information about which modality, encoder, or profile strategy contributes most to validation accuracy. The entire design space is unexplored. 2) What this tests: config_001 (rna_only, singleprofile, pca_n2000) is the simplest possible configuration—a linear PCA encoder applied to a single RNA profile with no image input. It establishes a clean performance baseline for the RNA modality under the most minimal assumptions. 3) Why it is the best first use of budget: As a fast, low-complexity baseline, it anchors every subsequent comparison: (a) swapping the RNA encoder (scvi, scgpt) tells us whether learned representations beat PCA; (b) moving to multiprofile + aggregation tells us whether multi-view profiling adds signal; (c) adding an image branch (image_only or multimodal) tells us whether the image modality contributes beyond RNA alone. Without this reference point, results from more complex configurations would be uninterpretable. Choosing the simplest baseline first maximizes the information gained per experiment under a tight budget.

Evidence: Only one experiment (config_001: rna_only, singleprofile, pca_n2000) has been completed, yielding a low validation accuracy of ~48.5% and F1 of ~46.4%, establishing a weak RNA-only baseline. This leaves the most critical design question unanswered: does the image modality carry meaningful predictive signal for this task? Question being tested: config_010 (image_only, singleprofile, resnet50) directly measures the standalone performance of the image modality with a well-established encoder, providing a second modality-specific baseline. Why this is the best next experiment: Before investing budget in multimodal fusion or more complex RNA encoders, we must know whether images are a viable signal source. If image_only performs comparably or better than RNA-only, multimodal configurations become the clear exploitation target. If it performs poorly, we redirect budget toward improving the RNA side (better encoders like scgpt, multiprofile aggregation). This single experiment maximally reduces uncertainty about the highest-level architectural decision (which modality to rely on) and will most efficiently guide all subsequent experiments under the limited budget.

We now have both unimodal baselines: RNA-only (pca_n2000, singleprofile) at 48.5% accuracy and image-only (resnet50, singleprofile) at 20.8%. The most critical question for this multimodal study is whether combining these two modalities yields any benefit over the stronger unimodal baseline. config_016 (multimodal, singleprofile, pca_n2000 + resnet50, concat) uses the exact same encoders as both completed experiments, making it a clean, single-variable test of fusion. If it exceeds 48.5%, multimodal is a promising direction and we should explore aggregation and better encoders; if it falls below, the weak image signal (20.8%) is likely to hurt rather than help, redirecting effort toward improving the image encoder or RNA multiprofile design. This experiment maximally reduces uncertainty about the central design decision (unimodal vs. multimodal) before spending budget on more complex configurations.

Evidence: config_016 (multimodal, PCA n2000 + ResNet50, concat) achieves 0.527 acc, outperforming RNA alone (0.485) and image alone (0.208). The image modality contributes ~4% in combination but is very weak standalone, suggesting ResNet50 may be underfitting the image signal. Question tested: config_022 swaps only the image encoder to ImageNet-pretrained ViT-L while keeping everything else identical to config_016 (single profile, PCA n2000, concat fusion), giving a clean single-variable test of whether a stronger image encoder increases the multimodal gain. Why best next: If ViT-L substantially lifts accuracy, it confirms the image encoder is the bottleneck and justifies exploring multiprofile/aggregation variants with ViT-L (configs 024-027). If it does not, we learn the image modality has a hard ceiling and should focus budget on RNA encoder upgrades or fusion strategy. This single experiment resolves a high-uncertainty design choice that gates many downstream configurations, making it the most budget-efficient next step.

Evidence: The current best is config_022 (multimodal, singleprofile, pca_n2000, imagenet_vit_l, concat) at 0.535 acc. RNA dominates over image (0.485 vs 0.208), and multimodal fusion adds ~5 points over RNA alone. The vit_l encoder slightly outperforms resnet50. However, all multimodal experiments so far use singleprofile; the impact of multiprofile with aggregation is completely untested and represents a major architectural decision. Question: Does switching from singleprofile to multiprofile with avgpool aggregation improve performance when combined with the best-known components (pca_n2000, imagenet_vit_l, concat)? Why this is the best next experiment: It extends the current best configuration with the simplest and most interpretable aggregation (avgpool), isolating the effect of multiprofile while holding all other variables at their best-known values. If multiprofile+avgpool helps, it opens the aggregation dimension (transformer) as a follow-up; if it hurts, we learn that singleprofile suffices and can redirect budget to fusion method or RNA encoder choices. This maximizes information gain per experiment under the limited budget.

Evidence: config_024 (multiprofile, pca_n2000, imagenet_vit_l, avgpool, concat) achieved 0.629 acc, a ~9.3% jump over the best singleprofile multimodal (config_022: 0.535), confirming multiprofile is the dominant design lever. The aggregation method (avgpool) is the one untested dimension within this best-performing family. Question: Does transformer-based aggregation of multiple profiles capture inter-profile structure that simple averaging misses, yielding further gains over 0.629? Why this experiment: config_026 is a clean single-variable extension of the current best (only aggregation changes from avgpool to transformer), giving a direct A/B comparison. If it improves, we identify a better aggregation strategy to build on; if it does not, we confirm avgpool is sufficient and can redirect budget toward RNA encoder or fusion-method variations. Under a tight budget, this maximizes information per experiment by isolating one hypothesis on the most promising configuration.

The current best is config_024 (multimodal, multiprofile, pca_n2000, imagenet_vit_l, avgpool, concat) at 0.629 acc, and all multimodal experiments so far have used concat fusion. The only untested fusion strategy is weighted, which directly tests whether the modality combination mechanism matters beyond simple concatenation. This is a clean single-variable change from the current best, so any performance shift can be cleanly attributed to fusion strategy. Given the limited budget, exploiting the strongest known direction (multiprofile + vit_l + avgpool) while resolving the fusion question is more informative than introducing an untested RNA encoder (scvi/scgpt) whose standalone performance is unknown. If weighted fusion improves on concat, we gain a better configuration immediately; if not, we confirm concat is sufficient and can redirect effort to RNA encoder choice.

The current best (config_025, acc=0.635) uses pca_n2000 as the RNA encoder, and all completed multimodal experiments share this encoder. We have zero evidence on whether a learned RNA encoder (scvi_n200) could improve the RNA representation in the multimodal context. The aggregation (avgpool > transformer) and fusion (weighted > concat) questions are relatively well-resolved with small deltas (~3-6%), but the RNA encoder is a major unexplored design axis with potentially larger impact. Config_037 (scvi_n200, imagenet_vit_l, avgpool, weighted) is a clean single-variable swap from the current best, directly testing whether a variational autoencoder-based RNA representation outperforms linear PCA. This is the highest-information experiment: it either reveals a new best configuration or confirms PCA is sufficient, and the answer will guide all subsequent encoder choices across the remaining search space.

The strongest evidence so far is that switching the RNA encoder from PCA (config_025, 0.6352) to scVI (config_037, 0.7062) yielded a ~7-point accuracy gain, confirming that a learned RNA representation is the most impactful design axis. However, we have only tested one learned encoder (scVI). Config_049 (scGPT, multiprofile, imagenet_vit_l, avgpool, weighted) isolates the question of whether the specific learned encoder matters or whether any learned representation suffices, while holding all other settings at their proven-best values. If scGPT matches scVI, we learn the key insight is 'use a learned encoder' and can redirect budget to other axes (e.g., aggregation). If scGPT underperforms, we confirm scVI's architecture is specifically important. This reduces uncertainty on the highest-leverage untested design dimension, making it the most informative use of the next experiment.

The current best is config_037 (scvi_n200, vit_l, multiprofile, avgpool, weighted; acc 0.706). With PCA, avgpool clearly outperformed transformer aggregation (config_024: 0.629 vs config_026: 0.599). However, scvi_n200 produces a structured, learned latent representation rather than a linear projection, so a transformer aggregator may be able to exploit inter-profile dependencies that simple averaging discards. Config_039 changes exactly one variable (avgpool→transformer) from the current best while keeping the proven scvi_n200 + vit_l + multiprofile + weighted backbone. If transformer matches or exceeds avgpool here, it reveals that the aggregation choice is encoder-dependent and opens a new design axis; if it underperforms, it confirms avgpool is robustly superior regardless of RNA encoder, reducing future search uncertainty. This is the highest-information single-step exploitation from the current best under a limited budget.
